query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal annealing treatment enhances the local chemical order and coherence at the FCC/BCC phase interfaces in the as‐deposited HEA protective coating, thereby increasing generalized planar fault energies that raise the activation barriers for dislocation motion and improve creep resistance under sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coating with dual-phase microstructure and inherent local chemical disorder at the interfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply a systematic thermal treatment (annealing) protocol designed to modify local chemical ordering and interface characteristics between the FCC and BCC grains.
generation.conditions: Creep regime under sustained loading at temperatures where time-dependent plasticity is prominent and microstructural evolution is active.
generation.structural_mediator: Optimized FCC/BCC interfaces with enhanced local chemical order that act as effective barriers to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced chemical order increases the generalized planar fault energies and creates a more rugged energy landscape, thereby increasing the lattice friction encountered by dislocations. This impedes dislocation glide and delays the transition to tertiary creep, resulting in improved creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the as-deposited baseline, thermally annealed coatings will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep rates and a delayed onset of tertiary creep under identical sustained stress conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as-deposited HEA coating with less optimized FCC/BCC interfaces and lower local chemical ordering.
generation.boundary: Improved performance is expected within the creep regime at moderate-to-elevated temperatures; however, if the applied stress or temperature exceeds material limits leading to phase degradation or interface weakening, the beneficial effects of annealing may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the creep resistance improvement is uncertain and likely to depend on the specific annealing parameters (e.g., temperature and duration) as well as the alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC HEA protective coatings: (1) control samples in the as-deposited state and (2) samples subjected to a defined annealing protocol to enhance local chemical order at the phase interfaces. Subject both sets to identical, controlled creep tests under sustained loading at regulated elevated temperatures.
measurements: Time to onset of tertiary creep
Microstructural characterization (e.g., via TEM or SEM) of FCC/BCC interfaces to assess changes in local chemical order and coherency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance (i.e., reduced creep rate and delayed tertiary creep onset) along with corresponding microstructural evidence of enhanced FCC/BCC interface quality compared to the as-deposited baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys under sustained high-temperature loads (as in PMC5627260) demonstrated that traditional creep tests can reveal the overall time‐dependent deformation behavior, with factors such as low stacking‐fault energy and evolving microstructural rafting playing dominant roles. Subsequently, studies like PMC6982153 used localized nanoindentation creep experiments to expose differences in dislocation creep between FCC and BCC (or BCC‐based) regions, elucidating how specific atomic packing and stacking interactions can control local deformation. However, these works typically examined bulk or nano‐scale responses without addressing a controlled alteration of the as‐deposited microstructure in dual-phase FCC/BCC coatings under continuous loading.
decision.unsolved: The specific mechanism that confers creep resistance in an as‐deposited FCC/BCC HEA coating remains unclear, particularly regarding the role of the local interface between FCC and BCC phases and the consequent dislocation blockage or phase transformation events under sustained, time‐dependent loading. In other words, while overall creep behavior and dislocation mechanisms have been characterized, it is still unresolved how variations in local chemical order or microstructural interfacing between FCC and BCC domains govern long‐term creep resistance, and what operating boundaries (e.g., thermal stress thresholds) might limit such performance.
decision.lever: Implement a thermal treatment (annealing) protocol to systematically modify the local chemical order and interface characteristics between the FCC and BCC grains in the as-deposited coating.
decision.why: Given that past studies identified microstructural features—such as stacking fault energies and dislocation interactions—that control creep behavior, the next logical step is to tune the FCC/BCC interface via controlled thermal processing. This controlled alteration will serve as an unspecified controlled comparison relative to the untreated baseline, thus enabling direct observation of changes in creep resistance (e.g., delayed onset of tertiary creep or modified strain rate under sustained stress) under defined operating boundaries. Such an approach also provides a clear falsification criterion: if the modified interface does not yield a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance compared to the baseline, the hypothesized role of local chemical order at FCC/BCC boundaries is refuted.
